subject: Initial thoughts on shiny, ggplot and d3

messages.author: c8fe4075ec631c03
messages.subject: Initial thoughts on shiny, ggplot and d3
parts:
I'm an avid user of Hadley Wickham's http://ggplot2.org, and I want to use the props thus developed to build shiny apps with d3.  This question has come up a couple times on the board, and I want to share my thoughts to spark a discussion of how to make this easy. 

I see 4 routes to this being a reality, with different pros and cons.

1) d3 Display backend to R.

Much like R can print to pdf, svg, png, cairo, add a d3 backend.  Interactivity would then have to either be automatic, or retrofitted to metadata in grid, ggplot etc.  This would be solid and widely compatible with R plot types

2) Grid to d3 converter.

Probably easier to write an initial version of, a function which takes a Grid object and sends the primitives to d3.  Likely to be a bulky data format, since the same data may be carried different ways (repeated grob descriptions, implied range in scales and plots etc).  It also would be more difficult to complete since grid is large and extensible.

Would work with lattice and ggplot, but not base plot

3) Ggplot_build to d3 converter

Once you have declaratively specified your plot in ggplot using geoms, scales, data, stats, position, facets and aesthetics, ggplot uses ggplot_build to internally process the data structures - and creates a new object with all of the work done.

This would be a neat place to intercede, although my initial pass over this wasn't as happy as I would like; the data is not truly meant to be human readable, some data is implicit or spread out, and it's possible the format will change in the future.

d3 would need methods for each of the geoms, scales etc, although a small initial working set wouldn't be too hard.  Also allows more flexibility in the form of the output - d3 can do things a bit differently.

Compatible with ggplot but not lattice or base.

4) Complete port of ggplot into d3.

In this scheme, you essentially send the unprocessed ggplot object (or just the declaration) up to d3, and it does all the work.  That's my current approach, since it gets d3 native performance and style, plus lots of flexibility.

Not really compatible with anything except my brain.

---

If I get around to it I'll send some code examples.

-Alex

Yes, I have had a look at that, and took a first pass at consuming some of it.  One challenge I encountered was that the data I need:

* aesthetic mapping
* raw data
* factor levels

are spread through the $data and $plot elements, and while most are present, it wasn't clear to me if I could reliably reconsititute them.

For example, in a bar chart the values ymin, dmax appear in the $data object.  However, they are generated by a stat, and it's not clear I can programmatically relate those back to the original named data item (they aren't in plot$mapping or plot$labels) without adding too much special knowledge in the decoder (visit the scale?).  PANEL is yet more complex; there IS NO aesthetic to map it back to.

In general this seems tractable and relatively attractive, though.

messages.author: c8fe4075ec631c03
messages.subject: Re: Initial thoughts on shiny, ggplot and d3
parts:
I have been mulling option 4 - re-implementing ggplot in d3, and I have come up with a few questions that I haven't yet worked out how to answer:

Should 'g2plot.js' be aimed at R users, or at d3/js users (or both)?  It might be usable for both either way, but we could think on the following issues:

  * Should we expect all data prep be done in R, or provide facilities to do data prep in JS? (think reshape, extending stat_* to be more complete, etc)
  * Should the input data be general, which is to say suitable for generating multiple plots, or should it be targeted at one plot style with a specific X and Y etc?
    This is related to the first point, since while the input data may be pre-processed in R, ggplot currently also expects you to walk some of the last 'half mile' using R, and that half mile differs depending upon the expected output.  Think re-ordering factor levels, adding annotations such as labels and lines for averages (and calculating the averages) etc.
  * Is the primary command UI an R facility or a JS facility?  This has a couple of issues - if we are aiming at R users, then familiarity with R conventions is a plus, either in the JS or R interface.  We might expect to provide JS proxies for R objects such as lists (ordered hashmaps) and data frames (column major typed 2d arrays).  If we are aiming at JS users, then the converse applies, and it may be a disadvantage to require use of proxies.
  * Should the JS be assembled by R, or be a client-side library.  The first option may be better in performance and more amenable to hacking once built.  The second option is more useful but may be opaque and difficult for users to augment with their own custom fun stuff.  This is related to the idea -
  * should the solution be (primarily) powerful with a clean R/JS command interface, or simple with a clean JS code structure (like d3, that's amenable to easy customisation)?  These things keep me awake at night :-)
  * Clearly it's cheaper to target one user base than both.

We also might consider if rebuilding ggplot-like facilities allows a re-think of some basics.  I'm sure everyone has some 'if-only' ideas, but I'd be pleased to see some of the following:

  * demotion of facets to an extension of aesthetics with special scale rules.  Ordinal (factor) aesthetics may be mapped in many ways to the plot - as a x,y,wrap,page! facet, as a group, as a nested x-axis, as a stacked y axis etc etc etc.  This is currently non-orthogonal in ggplot, and needs love.
  * expansion of stat_ to cover common cases such as adding a y-mean per group, or a floating label.  This may be particularly important for JS users, (or not) depending upon if they have the skills to do the client side data prep, and if the g2plot implementation is transparent enough to allow addition.
  * less controversial is a mechanism to combine aesthetics to express a large-valued dataset - extension of e.g. 'profession' into the cross product of colors, stripes, outlines etc.

A related but complex topic is that data.table - and CSVs are poor structural representations of real data (for all that they might be clean and performant).  This impacts a few things:

  1) the structure for the (efficient) transmission of data
  2) how to relate csv structured data to the underlying (more complex) data model.  Imagine expressing the columns of a csv as the terms of a GLM (or more!)- with all the operators in use - clustering, link functions, error models.  I may be talking out of my posterior here, but that's how i think actual data IS.  are the terms of an AES also the terms of a GLM?
  3) conversion of arbitrary formats to the row-major record oriented structure currently favoured by the d3 implementation.  (I'd like to work out how to do better in my d3 - and capture context from tree parents in nodes).

Some of the problems above suggest to me that there are two projects here:

 1) create a JS data (transmission, import and) manipulation library to solve some of the above
 2) build a grammar-of-graphics interface to d3 that meets at least some of the above.

Okay, that's enough from me; what are your thoughts on this?

-Alex

messages.subject: Re: Initial thoughts on shiny, ggplot and d3
parts: On Monday, January 7, 2013 10:19:20 PM UTC-8, Alex Brown wrote:
A related but complex topic is that data.table - and CSVs are poor structural representations of real data

The impact of this is that users have to laboriously re-inject the structure of the data, often on the graphing interface as they 'reshape' and apply aesthetics.  If we could copy the idea of the aesthetic and provide a 'structure()' mapping then that mapping could be moved away from the graphing interface, and allow informed reshape as well as better performance in processing and on-the wire.

-Alex

messages.subject: Re: Initial thoughts on shiny, ggplot and d3
parts:
I am the author of rCharts that Kenton mentioned in his post. Polychart, the JS library that is one of the many that works with rCharts, is based on grammar of graphics. In fact, the author of Polychart states that ggplot2 was her motivation when she built Polychart. I am in the process of recreating plots from the R cookbook using rCharts and Polychart and it seems like 90% of the capabilities are covered. 

Interactivity is already built into Polychart and rather simple to use. However, it still requires users to know a little bit of JS/Coffeescript. With `knitr` it is easy to seamlessly integrate everything. You can see an example of this here http://ramnathv.github.io/rChartsNYT/. The third graph has interactivity added using a bit of coffeescript, which knitr makes really easy to integrate.

The only hitch is with the license of Polychart. It is not free for commercial use.

I know that rCharts is not as robust a solution as r2d3 or gg2v will turn out to be. But, I am looking for feedback so that I can take rCharts to the best of what it can do. 

Ramnath

I am posting this reply here for the benefit of the group.

rCharts takes a very different approach to generating JS based charts. Essentially, everything happens within R. Every time the user changes an input, rCharts outputs a fresh set of JS code to the page. Since, everything happens within R, rCharts does not require any Shiny bindings. Note that bindings are required when you want R to talk to JS. rCharts directly generates the required JS and hence is not really talking with JS.

The page refresh is faster than generating an R plot, since we are only outputting text.

messages.subject: Re: Initial thoughts on shiny, ggplot and d3
parts:
G3plot's approach is to provide an interface using grammar of graphics but all the work is done in JavaScript.

It extends ggplot like capabilities by allowing interaction with the plot to talk to other plots and the server.

It can be used to build a web shiny application customised to your data set and r analyses without needing to learn JavaScript or d3, and very rapidly.

http://glimmer.rstudio.com/alexbbrown/g3plot/#dataSet=Indometh,tabSelected=G3Plot

Also take a look in GitHub (linked from above) and read Plots.R and PlotInputs.R.

There's no documentation right now beyond how to use it in your app.

-Alex

g3plot look terrific, and I look forward to playing with it and learning from the code. While, we are discussing features, I thought it would be good to point out what rCharts can do.

1. It can be used straight from R, without knowing any javascript or D3. Advance customization requires JS, but not terribly complicated.
2. It is not restricted to just d3.js. It support six JS libraries so far including Polychart, which is based on Grammar of Graphics.
3. It can be used to create standalone charts, shiny apps or in a webpage/slidify deck.

So in short, rCharts attempts to produce JS visualizations from R, using an interface already familiar to R users.

I put together a short demo video, which you can see here

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nYr5KzaR1Vc

messages.author: ca3205004f4bea24
messages.subject: Re: Initial thoughts on shiny, ggplot and d3
parts: Non-free licenses are a deal-breaker.
On Tue, Apr 23, 2013 at 9:30 AM, Ramnath Vaidyanathan <ramnath...@gmail.com> wrote:

I am the author of rCharts that Kenton mentioned in his post. Polychart, the JS library that is one of the many that works with rCharts, is based on grammar of graphics. In fact, the author of Polychart states that ggplot2 was her motivation when she built Polychart. I am in the process of recreating plots from the R cookbook using rCharts and Polychart and it seems like 90% of the capabilities are covered. 

Interactivity is already built into Polychart and rather simple to use. However, it still requires users to know a little bit of JS/Coffeescript. With `knitr` it is easy to seamlessly integrate everything. You can see an example of this here http://ramnathv.github.io/rChartsNYT/. The third graph has interactivity added using a bit of coffeescript, which knitr makes really easy to integrate.

The only hitch is with the license of Polychart. It is not free for commercial use.

I know that rCharts is not as robust a solution as r2d3 or gg2v will turn out to be. But, I am looking for feedback so that I can take rCharts to the best of what it can do. 

Ramnath
